name: Reciprocal interaction of ideas and circumstances
plain_explanation: Neither the view that great thinkers single-handedly change history, nor the view that ideas are mere passive 'froth' produced by material forces, is correct; ideas and practical life shape each other back and forth, like the chicken and the egg.
precise_definition: Russell's methodological thesis that between ideas and practical/social life there is reciprocal interaction, such that asking which is cause and which effect is as unanswerable in the abstract as the problem of the hen and the egg.
why_it_mattered: It frames Russell's entire historical method in this chapter and justifies studying liberalism concretely, through its actual seventeenth-to-twentieth-century development, rather than abstractly.
historical_origin: Presented by Russell as a corrective to two 'opposite errors, both common': overestimating philosophers' influence, and treating theorists as passive products of circumstance.
associated_philosopher: Bertrand Russell (methodological remark, not attributed to a historical philosopher)
examples: A political party claiming inspiration from a philosopher may really have acted as it would have anyway, with the philosopher only 'acclaimed' after the fact.
competing_positions: Pure materialism (ideas are epiphenomenal 'froth' on material/technical causes)
